title: "Lineage assignment"
subtitle: "Module 2 — 30 min"

## What is a lineage?

A lineage is a named group of genomes sharing a common ancestor, defined by **mutations specific to that group**
(Pango lineages, Nextstrain clades…). Names are hierarchical: `TV.2.1` descends from `TV.2`. Lineages give a common language
to talk about genomes without exchanging full sequences.

```bash
column -t data/outbreak/lineage_definitions.tsv
```

| Lineage | Parent | Defining SNPs |
|---|---|---|
| TV.1 | root | none (reference-like) |
| TV.2 | TV.1 | 8 SNPs |
| TV.2.1 | TV.2 | + 3 SNPs |
| TV.2.2 | TV.2 | + 3 other SNPs |
| TV.3 | TV.1 | 6 SNPs |

## Step 1 — Assign the lineages

We use a small program written for the course (a miniature Pangolin): for each genome it looks for the defining
SNPs and picks the **most specific** lineage whose SNPs are **all** present.

```bash
python3 scripts/13_lineage.py results/phylo/aln.fasta
```

**Questions**

1. What lineage is S01, and what is the evidence?
2. One genome has a masked defining SNP. What does the "evidence" column say? Is the call still reliable?
3. Make a table: number of genomes per lineage and per region.

(For question 3, join the lineages with the metadata:
`join -t $'\t' <(sort -k1,1 results/phylo/lineages.tsv) <(sort -k1,1 data/outbreak/metadata.tsv) | cut -f1,2,4,5 | sort -k2`.)

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers
1. **S01 = TV.2**, with evidence "8/8 defining SNPs". It does not carry the TV.2.1 or TV.2.2 SNPs, so it stays at the parent level.
2. **OB24** says "TV.2.2 – 10/11 defining SNPs, 1 masked": the 11th SNP lies in the block of N. All the 10 observed SNPs
   agree, so TV.2.2 is the best call, but it is **less certain** (missing data). Real tools such as Pangolin and Nextclade flag exactly this.
3. Number of genomes per lineage and region:

| Lineage | Region A | Region B | Region C | Region D |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TV.1 | – | 2 | – | 1 |
| TV.3 | – | 5 | – | – |
| TV.2 | 3 (+ S01) | – | 1 | – |
| TV.2.1 | 7 | – | 1 | – |
| TV.2.2 | – | – | 7 | – |
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Real tools
**Pangolin** and **Nextclade** do the same with much larger nomenclatures, and also give quality flags (missing data,
unexpected mutations, mixed sites). The principle — defining mutations, most specific complete match — is identical.
:::

## Final question

Can two genomes of the same lineage still be unrelated cases? Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer
Yes. A lineage is defined by **a few mutations**, and many separate chains of transmission can carry the same lineage
(for example if it was imported several times, or circulated widely before being sampled). A lineage says "belongs to this
family"; to say "linked case" you need **finer resolution** (extra SNPs, as in the SNP matrix) **and** epidemiological information
(dates, places, contacts).
:::
